period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, c. 1264-1244 BC
summary: Two temples cut into a Nubian cliff by Ramesses II, buried by sand for centuries, then sawn apart and rebuilt on higher ground in the 1960s.
look: You are on the west shore of Lake Nasser, with two temple fronts cut into the hill and facing east over the water. With the lake behind you, the Great Temple of Ramesses II and its four seated giants is on the left; the Small Temple of Hathor and Nefertari, with six standing figures, is about 100 m to the right. Both hills are artificial: concrete domes dressed with rock, built when the temples were moved in 1964-68.
story:
Ramesses II had both temples carved into a sandstone cliff above the Nile from about 1264 BC, and the work took around 20 years. This was Nubia, about 230 km south-west of Aswan as the crow flies and some 40 km from today's Sudanese border: the land that gave Egypt its gold. The Great Temple honours the state gods and Ramesses himself as a god; the Small Temple honours Hathor and his chief wife Nefertari. Anyone sailing north on the river met them first.

Then the desert moved in. By the 6th century BC sand already reached the colossi's knees. In March 1813 the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt climbed down to the small temple, turned south, and saw one giant head sticking out of a dune. In 1816 the French ex-consul Drovetti left 300 piastres with the local sheikh to pay for digging; the money came back untouched, because nobody saw the use of small metal discs. Giovanni Belzoni, a former circus strongman from Padua, persuaded them, and on 1 August 1817, after 22 days of shovelling, his party broke in. The first through the gap was the slimmest of them, Giovanni Finati, who found the air as hot and damp as a Turkish bath.

In September 1822 drawings of the cartouches here reached Jean-François Champollion in Paris; the first he read was the name Ramesses, a key moment in the decipherment of hieroglyphs. Six years later he crawled in himself, nearly naked, into 52 degrees of heat.

A good order for today: the Great Temple facade, its halls and sanctuary, then the Small Temple, then a look at the rescue. The facades face sunrise, so morning light is kindest. The Sun Festival, when the light reaches the sanctuary, falls on 22 October, five days after your visit.
details: Great Temple, second colossus from the left: its head and torso lie at its feet, probably felled by an earthquake soon after completion.
Above the Great Temple door: the falcon-headed sun god in his niche, the first figure Belzoni freed from the sand.
Small Temple, to the right: Queen Nefertari stands as tall as the king, a rare honour in Egyptian art.
The colossi's legs: graffiti from Greek mercenaries of about 593 BC and from 19th-century travellers.
The hill behind the facades: not a real mountain but rock fill over concrete domes from the 1960s rescue.
fun_fact: When Drovetti paid the local sheikh 300 piastres to dig out the door, the coins came back unspent: nobody in the village saw any use for them. Belzoni first had to convince the workmen that money was worth having.
narration: You are standing on the shore of Lake Nasser, looking at two temples cut into a cliff about 3,200 years ago. On the left is the Great Temple of Ramesses the Second, with its four seated giants. On the right, about 100 metres away, is the Small Temple, made for the goddess Hathor and for his wife Nefertari. Ramesses began the work around 1264 BC, and it took about 20 years. This was Nubia, the land of gold, and the temples were a message to anyone sailing on the river: Egypt is in charge here. Then the desert moved in. Sand buried the Great Temple until only one head stuck out. A Swiss traveller, Johann Burckhardt, spotted it in 1813. In 1817 Giovanni Belzoni, a former circus strongman, dug for 22 days to open a gap at the door. The thinnest man in the team crawled through first, into air as hot as a Turkish bath. A few years later, drawings of the royal names carved here helped Champollion crack hieroglyphs. In the 1960s a new dam was about to drown everything, so the temples were sawn into blocks and rebuilt on higher ground. Even the hill they sit in is man-made. Now look at the second giant from the left. His head and chest lie on the ground at his feet, exactly where they fell long ago.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, c. 1264-1244 BC
summary: Four 20-metre Ramesses sit in a row, one headless since antiquity, with his family at his knees and Greek soldiers' graffiti on his legs.
look: The facade is about 33 m high and 38 m wide, cut from the cliff and facing east to the sunrise. Four seated colossi of Ramesses II, each about 20 m tall, wear the double crown; the second from the left lost its head and torso, which lie at its feet. Small statues of his mother, wives and children stand between and beside the legs, none higher than his knees. Over the door the falcon-headed sun god stands in a niche, and a row of baboons runs along the top.
story:
All four giants are Ramesses, enthroned, hands on knees, staring across the river. Around his legs stands his family: his mother Mut-Tuya, his chief wife Nefertari, his eldest sons Amun-her-khepeshef and Ramesses, and daughters including Bintanath, Nebettawy, Meritamen and Isetnofret. Not one of them reaches above his knee. That is the point.

Look up at the niche over the door. The falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty, crowned with a sun disc, holds a staff topped by an animal head, the hieroglyph user, 'strong', and a small figure of Maat, goddess of truth. Read together: User-Maat-Ra, the throne name of Ramesses II. On either side the king offers to the god, so Ramesses is in effect worshipping his own name. The Greeks later heard that name as Ozymandias. Along the cornice, 22 baboons raise their paws to the rising sun, as baboons in the wild chatter at dawn.

The second colossus from the left broke, probably in an earthquake not long after it was finished. During the 1960s move the engineers chose not to restore it: the fallen head and torso were set back at its feet in the positions where they had been found.

The legs carry the oldest visitors' book in Nubia. Around 593 BC Pharaoh Psamtik II sent an army deep into Kush, and his Greek and Carian mercenaries scratched their names on the left leg of the colossus just south of the door. The Greek text says they came with King Psammetichus to Elephantine and sailed on beyond Kerkis 'as far as the river permits'. It is signed by Archon son of Amoibichos and Pelekos son of Eudamos, and is among the oldest Greek writing that can be dated so closely. In December 1845 Isabella Romer, the first European woman known to visit, cut her name into the throne of the southern colossus.
details: Second colossus from the left: the fallen head and torso at its feet, put back exactly as found during the 1960s move.
Above the door: falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty holding the user staff and a small Maat, a rebus of the king's name User-Maat-Ra.
Very top of the facade: the row of 22 baboons with raised paws, greeting the sunrise.
Left leg of the broken colossus: Greek mercenary graffiti of about 593 BC, among Carian and much later scratches.
Between and beside the legs: Nefertari and the queen mother Tuya, small figures that barely reach the king's knee.
fun_fact: The Greek soldiers who signed this leg around 593 BC were tourists of a sort, and so was every Victorian who added a name later. Please let the tradition end with them.
narration: In front of you sit four giants, each about 20 metres tall, and every one of them is Ramesses the Second. He wears the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt and stares east, over the water, at the sunrise. Around his legs stand his family: his mother Tuya, his queen Nefertari, his sons and daughters. Not one of them reaches higher than his knee. That was the message. Look up above the door. The falcon-headed sun god stands in a niche, holding a staff with an animal head in one hand and the little goddess of truth, Maat, in the other. Put them together and they spell User Maat Ra, the throne name of Ramesses. The Greeks later turned that name into Ozymandias. Along the very top, a row of baboons lift their paws to greet the rising sun. Now find the second giant from the left. He lost his head and chest, probably in an earthquake soon after the work was done. In the 1960s the engineers left him broken and put the pieces back at his feet, as they were found. Around 593 BC, Greek soldiers serving Pharaoh Psamtik scratched a message on his left leg, signed by Archon, son of Amoibichos, and Pelekos, son of Eudamos. It is some of the oldest closely dated Greek writing anywhere. Look for the small Greek letters on that leg.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II, year 34 (c. 1245 BC)
summary: A stela that turns a hard-won diplomatic marriage into a tale of Hittite surrender, the happy ending of the oldest surviving peace treaty.
look: The stela is cut into the rock face at the south end of the terrace, to the left of the four colossi as you face them. It is a tall, round-topped panel: a scene at the top, with the enthroned king receiving the Hittite ruler and his daughter, and a long, weathered hieroglyphic text below. Low side light brings the figures out best.
story:
In 1274 BC Ramesses fought the Hittites at Kadesh in Syria and nearly lost. The war dragged on for about 15 more years until, around 1259 BC, in the 21st year of his reign, he made a treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III. It is the oldest surviving peace treaty and the only one from the ancient Near East known from both sides: the Egyptian text is carved at Karnak and the Ramesseum, the Hittite one survives on clay tablets from Hattusa in Turkey. A copy hangs at the United Nations in New York.

The wedding came 13 years later. The letters survive, and they are very human: Ramesses complains about delays; Queen Puduhepa answers that her daughter needs a proper dowry, which takes time to gather. In autumn 1246 BC the princess left Hattusa with gold, silver, bronze, cattle and slaves, and reached Pi-Ramesses that winter. She became a Great Royal Wife with a new name, Maathorneferure, 'she who sees Horus, the beauty of Ra'.

This stela tells it the Egyptian way. Hattusili comes in person, bringing his goods as tribute and his eldest daughter as a gift, and Ramesses' prayer to the god Seth calms the winter weather for her journey. In reality the Hittite king never came. Same event, two press releases.
details: Top of the stela: Ramesses enthroned, with the Hittite king and his daughter approaching him.
The long text below: the wedding told as a Hittite submission, with Seth calming the winter weather.
Compare with the Kadesh reliefs inside the hall: the war first, then the peace that followed it.
On the 22nd at Karnak: the Egyptian text of the treaty is carved on an outer wall south of the Great Hypostyle Hall.
fun_fact: The treaty was originally engraved on silver tablets, one for each king. Both are lost; we read it today from temple walls in Luxor and clay tablets dug up in Turkey in 1906.
narration: On the rock face here, at the south end of the terrace, is a carved stela about a royal wedding. In 1274 BC Ramesses fought the Hittites at Kadesh and nearly lost. The war ground on for about 15 more years. Then, around 1259 BC, he and the Hittite king Hattusili signed a treaty: the oldest peace treaty that survives. A copy hangs today at the United Nations. Thirteen years later came the marriage that sealed it. The letters between the two courts survive, and they are very human. Ramesses complains about delays. The Hittite queen replies that her daughter needs a proper dowry, and that takes time. The princess finally came to Egypt with gold, silver, cattle and soldiers, and got a new Egyptian name, Maathorneferure. Now read the stela's version. Here the Hittite king comes in person, bringing his treasure and his eldest daughter as tribute, and Ramesses prays to the god Seth to calm the winter weather for them. He never came. Look at the scene at the top, where the Hittite king and his daughter approach the enthroned pharaoh.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Ramesses II; Battle of Kadesh 1274 BC
summary: Eight giant Ramesses as Osiris hold up the roof while the walls tell, comic-strip style, the battle he nearly lost at Kadesh.
look: Inside the door is a hall about 18 m long and 17 m wide, cut from solid rock. Eight pillars, four on each side, carry standing statues of Ramesses as Osiris with arms crossed: those on the left (south) wear the white crown of Upper Egypt, those on the right (north) the double crown. The whole right-hand wall is the Battle of Kadesh; the left-hand wall shows other wars. Beyond is a smaller hall with four pillars.
story:
The pillar statues show the king as Osiris, god of the dead and of renewal, holding crook and flail. Above the central aisle the vultures of the goddess Nekhbet spread their wings. Small side rooms opening off the hall were storerooms for temple equipment. In the second hall Ramesses and Nefertari stand before the sacred boat of the god.

The north wall is the star. In May 1274 BC, in year 5 of his reign, Ramesses marched into Syria with four divisions named after gods: Amun, Ra, Ptah and Seth. Near Kadesh on the river Orontes, two nomads told him the Hittite army was far away at Aleppo. They were Hittite plants. Ramesses pitched camp. Then two enemy scouts were caught and beaten until they talked: King Muwatalli II and his allies were hiding just behind the city. Hittite chariots smashed into the Egyptian army and broke into the camp. Ramesses charged with his bodyguard and held on until reinforcements arrived from the coast.

With 5,000 to 6,000 chariots in all, it was probably the largest chariot battle ever fought, and the first battle whose tactics we can follow. It ended in a stalemate: the Hittites kept Kadesh and pushed the border south. Ramesses came home and carved a victory on his temples, with himself alone against thousands, the hero of his own poem.

The south wall shows the more routine business of empire: the king storming a Syrian fortress and campaigning against Libyans and Nubians. You will meet the Kadesh story again at the Ramesseum on the 21st and on the outer wall of Karnak on the 22nd.
details: Left (south) row of Osiride pillars: the tall white crown; right (north) row: the double crown.
North (right) wall: the Egyptian camp, drawn as a rectangle of shields with horses and chariots resting inside.
Same wall: the two Hittite scouts being beaten with sticks, the moment the king learns the truth.
Same wall, higher up: the king in his chariot shooting arrows, and the Orontes looping round the walled city of Kadesh.
Central aisle ceiling: the outspread wings of Nekhbet's vultures.
fun_fact: Ramesses had this battle carved on several of his temples as a great victory, yet the Hittites kept Kadesh and the war dragged on for years. It may be the most expensive spin campaign in the ancient world.
narration: You are inside the first hall, cut straight out of the rock. Eight statues of Ramesses as Osiris hold up the roof, arms crossed over their chests. On your left they wear the tall white crown of the south, on your right the double crown. Above the middle aisle, vultures spread their wings across the ceiling. Now turn to the right-hand wall. This is the Battle of Kadesh, told like a comic strip. In 1274 BC, Ramesses marched into Syria with four divisions named after gods: Amun, Ra, Ptah and Seth. Near the city of Kadesh, two nomads told him the Hittite army was far away. They were Hittite spies. He made camp. Then his men caught two enemy scouts and beat the truth out of them: the Hittites were hiding right behind the city. Too late. Hittite chariots smashed into the army and broke into the camp. Ramesses charged with his bodyguard and held on until reinforcements arrived. It was probably the largest chariot battle ever fought, and in the end it was a draw. The Hittites kept Kadesh. Ramesses went home and carved a triumph on his temples. Look for the camp, drawn as a rectangle of shields with horses inside, and the two scouts being beaten with sticks.

summary: At the back of the mountain four gods sit in the dark; twice a year the sunrise reaches three of them and leaves the fourth in shadow.
look: The sanctuary is a small room at the very back, on a straight line from the door, about 60 m into the rock. Four seated statues carved from the living rock sit against the back wall: from left to right Ptah, Amun-Ra, the deified Ramesses and Ra-Horakhty. They are worn, so look for shapes rather than faces. The stone block in front of them is the stand for the god's sacred boat.
story:
This is the temple's heart. The great state gods sit here together: Ptah of Memphis, Amun-Ra of Thebes and Ra-Horakhty, the rising sun of Heliopolis. Between them, as an equal, sits Ramesses himself. A living king placing himself in his own holy of holies was bold even by pharaoh standards.

The temple's axis points at the sunrise. Around 22 February and 22 October the first rays run the whole length of the temple, through both halls, and light the back wall. Amun-Ra, Ramesses and Ra-Horakhty are lit; Ptah, a god often linked with the underworld, stays in shadow. Amelia Edwards, the Victorian traveller who later founded the Egypt Exploration Fund, watched the beam and was convinced it was a calculated effect.

Two stories often come with the dates. One says they were Ramesses' birthday and coronation day: there is no direct evidence for that. The other says the 1960s move shifted the dates by a day. In fact the engineers watched the light reach the statues in the original temple on 22 February 1966, before it was cut, and set out the rebuilt temple to repeat it, to a tolerance of a few millimetres. Over 3,000 years the slow wobble of the Earth's axis has probably shifted the effect more than the move did.

On festival mornings thousands of people queue in the dark to see it. You are here five days before the October date, which means fewer elbows.
details: Far left: Ptah, the one god the sun never reaches.
Second from the right: Ramesses himself, seated as an equal among the gods.
Far right: falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty, the same rising-sun god who stands over the front door.
The block in front of the statues: the stand where the god's sacred boat rested.
Turn round: the dark rooms, the bright doorway and the lake beyond sit on one straight line.
fun_fact: When they rebuilt the temple 65 metres higher, the engineers set its orientation to within about 5 millimetres, so that the sun would still find the same three gods.
narration: You have reached the sanctuary, the deepest room of the temple, about 60 metres inside the rock. Four figures sit against the back wall. From left to right: Ptah, the creator god of Memphis. Amun Ra, king of the gods, from Thebes. Then Ramesses himself, sitting with the gods as one of them. And on the right, the falcon-headed sun god, Ra Horakhty. The faces are worn, so look for the shapes. Now the famous trick. The temple is aimed at the sunrise. Around the 22nd of February and the 22nd of October, the first rays run the whole length of the temple, through both halls, and light up this back wall. Amun, Ramesses and the sun god shine. Ptah, a god often linked with the underworld, stays in shadow. You may hear that these dates were the king's birthday and coronation. There is no evidence for that. You may also hear that the 1960s move shifted the dates by a day. In fact the engineers watched the light reach these statues on 22 February 1966, before they cut the temple apart, and aimed the rebuilt one to repeat it. The festival this year is on the 22nd, five days from now, with thousands of people queueing in the dark. Turn around now and look back: the dark halls, the bright doorway and the lake beyond sit on one straight line.

summary: A temple for a queen: on its facade Nefertari stands as tall as Ramesses, an honour almost no other Egyptian queen received.
look: About 100 m north of the Great Temple, the facade holds six standing statues a little over 10 m tall, set between deep buttresses: on each side of the door a statue of Nefertari between two of Ramesses. She wears Hathor's cow horns, sun disc and tall plumes; small figures of their children stand at the knees. Inside is a hall of six pillars with Hathor-faced capitals, a cross-room, and a small sanctuary with the cow of Hathor in the back wall.
story:
Nefertari was Ramesses' first Great Royal Wife, and this temple belongs to her and to the goddess Hathor. It is only the second Egyptian temple we know of dedicated to a queen, after Akhenaten's temple for Nefertiti. In Egyptian art size means rank, and queens normally stand knee-high beside their husbands, as they do next door. Here she is the same height as the king. The dedication calls her, in a well-known translation, the one for whom the sun shines.

Inside, the six pillars carry Hathor's face with cow's ears, shaped like the handle of the sistrum, the rattle her priestesses shook. On the walls Nefertari offers flowers and plays the sistrum; in one scene the goddesses Isis and Hathor crown her; in another Ramesses smites an enemy before the gods while the queen stands behind him. In the sanctuary niche Hathor appears as a cow stepping out of the mountain, the 'Mistress of the temple'.

Nefertari fades from the record not long after the temples were inaugurated, around year 24 of the reign, and she may not have lived to see much of their life. On the 21st you can visit her tomb, Q V 66 in the Valley of the Queens, where she appears again, painted, playing board games and meeting the gods.
details: Facade: Nefertari, the middle figure on each side, as tall as the king, with Hathor's horns, sun disc and plumes.
At the knees of the giants: small figures of their sons and daughters, arranged symmetrically.
Hall pillars: the face of Hathor with cow's ears at the top, like the handle of a sistrum rattle.
Inner walls: Nefertari between Isis and Hathor, who place a crown on her head.
Sanctuary back wall: the cow of Hathor stepping out of the rock.
fun_fact: Nefertari's name means 'beautiful companion'. Ramesses had several Great Royal Wives over his long reign, but she is the one who got a temple of her own.
narration: This is the Small Temple, made for the goddess Hathor and for Nefertari, the first chief wife of Ramesses. Count the six figures on the facade, each a little over 10 metres tall. Four are Ramesses. Two, the middle figure on each side, are Nefertari, dressed as Hathor with cow horns, a sun disc and two tall feathers. Here is the remarkable thing: she is exactly as tall as the king. In Egyptian art, size means rank, and queens normally stand knee-high beside their husbands, like the little ones next door. This is only the second temple we know of dedicated to a queen. Its inscription calls her the one for whom the sun shines. Inside, the pillars carry the face of Hathor with cow's ears, shaped like the rattle her priestesses shook. On the walls Nefertari offers flowers and shakes her own rattle, and two goddesses, Isis and Hathor, place a crown on her head. At the back, Hathor appears as a cow stepping out of the mountain. Nefertari fades from the record soon after these temples were finished. On the 21st you can see her tomb in the Valley of the Queens, Q V 66, still bright with colour. Before you go in, look at the small figures at the giants' knees: their children, standing guard.

summary: In the 1960s engineers sawed both temples into 1,036 blocks, lifted them 65 metres up the hill and rebuilt them inside a man-made mountain.
look: Everything here was rebuilt. The cliff around the facades is a skin of rock over two concrete domes; the Great Temple's dome spans 55 m. Look closely at the facades, walls and ceilings and you can find the thin straight joints where the blocks were cut and fitted back together. With your back to the temples, the original site lies about 65 m lower and some 200 m out, under the lake.
story:
The Aswan High Dam would raise the water at Abu Simbel by up to 60 m. In 1959 Egypt asked UNESCO for help, and in March 1960 UNESCO launched its appeal to save the monuments of Nubia. The French Egyptologist Christiane Desroches Noblecourt and the Egyptian culture minister Tharwat Okasha drove it; Jacqueline Kennedy lobbied her husband for American money.

The proposals were wild: a dam around the temples, leaving them underwater for visitors to view, or an Italian plan to jack up the whole Great Temple, about 250,000 tons, in one piece. In 1963 Egypt chose the Swedish firm VBB's cheaper plan: cut the temples apart.

First a cofferdam held back the rising river and 31,000 tons of sand were dumped against the facades to protect them. Workers removed about 300,000 tons of rock from above. Then they sawed: interior blocks were limited to 20 tons, facade blocks to 30, and cuts were kept to about 6 mm. In all 1,036 blocks were numbered, lifted and stored. The Great Temple was rebuilt 65 m higher and about 200 m inland, aimed at the sunrise to within about 5 mm, roofed with a concrete dome and covered with an artificial hill. It was inaugurated on 22 September 1968, 18 months early, at a cost of about 42 million dollars, half paid by Egypt.

Egypt thanked the donors with four temples: Debod went to Madrid, Dendur to the Metropolitan Museum in New York, Taffeh to Leiden and Ellesyia to Turin. The campaign also led to the 1972 World Heritage Convention: the idea that some places belong to everyone.
details: Facade and inner walls: thin straight joint lines crossing the carving, where the saw cuts were made.
The broken colossus: its fallen head and torso were put back on the ground exactly where they lay before the move.
The hill: rock fill heaped over concrete domes, a mountain made in the 1960s.
Look out at the lake: the original site is under the water, about 65 m below the present terrace.
If a door into the dome behind the temple is open, peek in: it is the concrete shell that carries the hill.
fun_fact: Before cutting began, workers buried the facades under 31,000 tons of sand to protect them. After 150 years of digging it out, the temple was buried again on purpose.
narration: Everything around you was moved here between 1964 and 1968. The cliff is man-made: a skin of rock over two huge concrete domes. In the 1950s Egypt decided to build the High Dam at Aswan. Its lake would rise up to 60 metres here and drown both temples. So in 1960 UNESCO launched a worldwide appeal. The ideas were wild. A dam around the temples. Leaving them underwater for visitors to view. Jacking up the entire Great Temple, a quarter of a million tons, in one piece. In the end Egypt chose the cheaper plan, from a Swedish firm: cut the temples into blocks and rebuild them higher up. First, workers buried the facades under sand again to protect them. Then they cleared the rock above and began to saw, keeping the cuts to about 6 millimetres. Blocks weighed up to 30 tons. In all there were 1,036 of them, each numbered, lifted and stored. The Great Temple was rebuilt 65 metres higher and about 200 metres back from the water, and aimed at the sunrise to within a few millimetres. The rescue cost about 42 million dollars. Egypt thanked the donor countries with temples: one stands today in Madrid, another in New York. Now look closely at the facade for thin straight lines crossing the stone. Those are the saw cuts.

summary: The lake in front of you is a drowned country: some 480 km of Nubian villages, palm groves and monuments lie beneath it.
look: Turn your back to the temples and you face Lake Nasser, the reservoir of the Aswan High Dam. It is about 479 km long and up to 16 km wide; you are near its southern end, with Sudan only about 40 km away. Under the water in front of you lies the old Nile valley, including the spot where the temples stood until 1964.
story:
The High Dam was built between 1960 and 1970 and inaugurated in 1971. It ended the yearly flood that had shaped Egyptian life for millennia, gave the country water all year round and, at first, up to half its electricity. Behind it rose a lake of 5,250 square km, most of it in Egypt; the Sudanese call their southern part Lake Nubia.

The price was Nubia. Tens of thousands of Nubians, by many estimates around 100,000 people in Egypt and Sudan together, left their villages for good. In Egypt most were resettled on new land around Kom Ombo, which you pass on the 20th; in Sudan many went to Khashm el-Girba, far to the east. Houses, palm groves, graves and the river bank itself disappeared. Twenty-two monuments were moved in the UNESCO campaign; others, like the fortress of Buhen, are still underwater.

The lake has a life of its own now: 52 species of fish, fishing camps and Nile crocodiles. When the water is high it spills west into the desert and has created the Toshka lakes. The Nubian Museum in Aswan, on the 19th, tells the human side of this story.
details: Out on the water: the original temple site, about 65 m below the terrace and some 200 m out.
The shoreline: bare rock to the water's edge; the old green strip of the valley is all underwater.
Fishing boats, if you see any: tilapia and Nile perch are the main catch.
On the 19th: the Nubian Museum in Aswan tells the story of the lost villages.
fun_fact: At high water the lake overflows westward into the Sahara through a spillway and has made the Toshka lakes: new lakes in the middle of the desert.
narration: Turn your back to the temples and look at the water. This is Lake Nasser, the reservoir behind the Aswan High Dam, and it is about 480 kilometres long. Before the 1960s there was no lake here. There was the Nile, a thin green strip of palm groves, fields and Nubian villages, and these temples sat on its bank, 65 metres below where you stand. The dam was built between 1960 and 1970. It ended the yearly flood, gave Egypt water all year round, and at first produced up to half of the country's electricity. The price was Nubia. Tens of thousands of Nubians, by many estimates around 100,000 people in Egypt and Sudan, had to leave their homes. In Egypt most were resettled near Kom Ombo, which you will pass on the 20th. Some monuments were saved and moved. Others, like the fortress of Buhen, are still down there. The lake now holds 52 kinds of fish, and Nile crocodiles. Look out across the water and picture the old valley floor far below: houses, graves and fields, all still there in the dark.

period: New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC; Ramesses II 1279-1213 BC
summary: Abu Simbel stands not in Egypt's heartland but in Nubia, the land of gold, and that is exactly why Ramesses put his biggest faces here.
look: Look at the Great Temple facade the way an ancient boatman did: from the river, coming north from deeper Africa. The four colossi face east over the water, the first great image of Egyptian power a traveller met. South of you lies Sudan, the old land of Kush.
story:
Nubia is the Nile valley south of Aswan, broken by rocky cataracts. Egyptians called the northern part Wawat and the southern part Kush, and the whole region Ta-Seti, 'the land of the bow', for its archers. It sent north gold above all, plus ivory, ebony, incense, animal skins and soldiers. The Egyptian word for gold was nub, and many link the name Nubia to it, though that is not certain.

Around 1500 BC Thutmose I crushed the Nubian kingdom of Kerma, and for about four centuries Egypt ruled the region through a governor with the title King's Son of Kush, the viceroy. Ramesses II filled Nubia with temples, at least seven: Beit el-Wali, Gerf Hussein, Wadi es-Sebua, Derr, the two at Abu Simbel and more. In several of them the living king is worshipped as a god beside Amun, Ra and Ptah, as you saw in the sanctuary.

They were statements of control. A trader bringing gold north passed a mountain with the king's face on it four times. Nobody needed to read to get the message. The tables turned later: in the 8th century BC kings from Kush conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty.
details: The facade: the colossi face east across the water, where traders and gold boats once passed.
Sanctuary: Ramesses seated as a god among Amun, Ra and Ptah, the theology behind these Nubian temples.
Hall, south wall: the king's campaigns, including against Nubians, the force behind the message.
On the 19th: the Nubian Museum in Aswan tells the same centuries from the Nubian side.
fun_fact: Foreign kings constantly begged Pharaoh for gold. In the Amarna letters a Babylonian king even complained that a shipment shrank badly when melted down, and much of that gold came from Nubia.
narration: Why carve the biggest statues of your reign here, so far south? Because this was Nubia, and Nubia meant gold. The Nile south of Aswan ran through a narrow land the Egyptians called Kush and Wawat, or simply the land of the bow, for its famous archers. From here came gold, ivory, ebony, incense, animal skins and soldiers. Around 1500 BC Pharaoh Thutmose the First crushed the Nubian kingdom of Kerma, and for about four centuries Egypt ruled the region through a governor called the King's Son of Kush. Ramesses the Second covered it with temples, at least seven of them, and in several he is worshipped as a god. Think of this facade as a billboard on the river. A trader sailing north with a cargo of gold would come round the bend and see the king's face four times, each 20 metres high, staring down at him. Nobody needed to read hieroglyphs to get the message. Centuries later the tables turned, and kings from Kush conquered Egypt itself. Look at the colossi now and imagine seeing them from a small boat on the water below.
